title: A Postcard for the Summer
premise: Cellist Noor Hartwell, whose career ended in a humiliating final performance and a broken engagement she never mourned aloud, returns to her late grandmother's coastal house to settle the estate. There she finds an undelivered postcard from eleven years ago — written by her grandmother to a man wrongfully imprisoned for a crime the family's silence helped conceal. As Noor tracks down the man's son, Elias, a luthier with every reason to hate her name, she uncovers the truth of what her grandmother witnessed and chose not to report. Choosing justice over inheritance, Noor testifies to reopen the case, forfeiting the house that was her last tie to belonging. The novel ends with Elias teaching her to build rather than perform: a cello made from salvaged wood, played badly and joyfully in his workshop, as the postcard is finally delivered.
about_author: Kestrel Reyes is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade cataloguing other people's music before writing her own stories. She lives near the sea, where she collects postcards she never sends.

chapters.title: The Unsent Address
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Arriving at the decaying beach house to inventory her grandmother's estate, Noor finds a postcard dated eleven years ago, addressed to a stranger at a prison, never mailed. Reading it, she learns her grandmother confessed to witnessing something she stayed silent about. Emotional beat: dread disguised as grief; the past tense of Noor's own life begins to crack open.

chapters.title: What the Wood Remembers
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, with one interlude from Elias's journal. She seeks out Elias Vane, son of the imprisoned man, who repairs instruments in a town that remembers her grandmother fondly and his father as a thief. He recognizes her surname and shuts the door. She returns anyway, offering the postcard. Emotional beat: collision of guilt and defensiveness; two people guarding the same wound from opposite sides.

chapters.title: Eleven Summers of Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Together they reconstruct the night of the crime through letters, a neighbor's fading memory, and the grandmother's hidden ledger proving the real culprit was the family's business partner. When the statute clock on reopening the case begins closing, Noor must choose: testify and lose the inheritance funding her appeal-free life, or keep the silence she inherited. Emotional beat: rising terror and resolve; love arriving uninvited in the present tense.

chapters.title: Delivered
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. In a small hearing room, Noor testifies, surrendering the house and her last claim to safe belonging; Elias's father is exonerated weeks later. Grieving and unmoored, Noor finds Elias has kept the postcard framed above his workbench. He hands her a half-built cello and asks her to finish it with him. Emotional beat: forgiveness of the self in the mirror; belonging rebuilt by hand, offstage, out of time.
